posts.text:
Bought health insurance today, covered from tomorrow? Usually no.

Most plans have an initial wait of roughly 30 days for illness. Some listed illnesses and pre-existing diseases can have longer waits. Exact timelines vary, so check the policy wording.

Save this.

“My employer cover is enough” is a risky myth.
Another big one: “If I hide an old condition now, I can fix it at claim time.”
Usually not. If it was diagnosed or treated in the last 36-48 months, disclose it. Exact window is policy-specific. Save this.

Flying to Europe soon?

For a Schengen visa, your travel medical insurance usually needs about 30,000 euros of medical cover, valid across the Schengen area, and repatriation cover.

Check the policy wording. #TravelInsurance

A sprained ankle abroad can turn into a very expensive hospital visit.

Travel medical insurance can cover hospitalisation, emergency treatment, and often medical evacuation.

Before you fly, save the assistance number and policy copy offline. Save this. #TravelInsurance

Cheapest plan = best plan.

Usually, a lower premium means something was trimmed: co-pay, sub-limits, room caps, or narrower coverage.

Compare protection first, price second. Check the policy wording.

Follow for one clear insurance idea a day.

“Insurance companies never pay claims” is a lazy myth.

Most claims are paid. The ugly part is this: many disputes start with non-disclosure, waiting periods, or exclusions.

Tell the truth, keep records, check the policy wording. Save this.

Picking a round number for term cover is guesswork.

A simple start: annual income × years left to retirement, + outstanding loans, - existing assets and cover.

That is closer to your family's gap. Ask me anything about health cover.

10-15x income is a starting point, not a formula.

Add home and personal loans. Add more if you're the only earner.

Then ask the real question: without your income, how will monthly expenses run?

Save this.

Deluxe room at admission can shrink your claim.

If your policy allows only a single private AC room, taking a higher room category can trigger proportionate deduction across the bill, not just room rent.

Check the room cap before admission. Save this.

Rs 5 lakh hospital bill. You have insurance. Still paying Rs 1 lakh yourself?

That is what a 20% co-pay does. It cuts every claim, not just the premium.

Cheaper premium can mean costlier claim day. Check the policy wording. Save this.

Medical emergency? In the first hour, do 3 things:
Save the insurer helpline and policy number on your phone.
Tell the hospital you have insurance and want cashless.
Ask the insurance desk to start pre-authorisation.
Save this.

Cashless approval is not final claim settlement.

At admission, you show your health card. The hospital sends a pre-authorisation request to the insurer or TPA. Approval usually comes with a sanctioned amount, which can change later when the final bill is reviewed.

Save this.

Wealth building starts after protection, not before.

One hospitalisation or the loss of an earner can undo years of saving.
Insurance is what keeps the rest of the plan standing when life interrupts it.

Follow for one clear insurance idea a day.

Your health cover can get smaller without changing at all.

Medical inflation usually runs ahead of general inflation, so a cover fixed years ago may buy less hospital protection today than you think.

Save this.

Marriage. Baby. Home loan. Job change.

These are not just life updates. They change your liabilities and can change your group cover too.

Insurance is not a one-time purchase. Revisit the setting when life changes. Save this.

Lower premium always means smarter buy.

A deductible is the part you agree to pay before insurance pays anything. That is why top-up plans look cheap too.

Good only if that cash is actually set aside. Check the policy wording. Save this.

Cashless works everywhere if you have health insurance.

Not true. Cashless admission is only at hospitals on the insurer or TPA network. Outside that, the same treatment becomes reimbursement.

Before you buy, check nearby hospitals. Recheck yearly. Save this.

At admission, one question matters: cashless or reimbursement?

Cashless: insurer pays the hospital directly; you pay the non-payable part.
Reimbursement: you pay first, then file with every original bill.

Know this before the emergency. Save this.

Trip cancelled, so insurance will pay? Not always.

Cancellation cover usually pays only for listed reasons like illness, a death in the family, or certain travel disruptions. Change of mind is usually not one of them. Keep documents. Check the policy wording.

Save this.

Lost bag? Your claim can fail before it starts.

At the airport, file the airline Property Irregularity Report before you leave. Baggage cover usually needs that report, and expensive items may need receipts too. Sub-limits apply. Save this.

Lost passport abroad? Travel insurance is not only for hospital bills.

Some plans also cover passport replacement costs and emergency travel to get a new one, usually within a limit. Rare benefit, huge help on a bad day.

Save this.

Myth: my company covers me, so I am done.

Office cover usually ends with the job, can be modest, and may not extend well to parents. Personal cover stays with you across job changes.

Use both. Benefit + backup, not either/or.

Save this.

Young and healthy, so insurance can wait.

Myth.

The best time to buy is often when you are easiest to underwrite. Later, age raises premiums, and a new diagnosis can lead to exclusions, loading, or even a decline.

Save this.

“Nothing came back, so term insurance was a waste” is the myth.

Term insurance is the fee you pay so your family does not face the version of life where you are not there.

If it never pays out, that is the good outcome.

Save this.

Term plan covers risk. Investment plan tries to cover risk and grow money.

Usually, doing both in one policy means higher cost for smaller cover and modest returns.

Separate the jobs for clarity. Some still prefer the bundled discipline. Save this.

What decides your term premium?

Age, health history, tobacco use, income proof, cover amount, and policy term.

The part you can still act on today: don't wait, and don't hide smoking or tobacco use.

Follow for one clear insurance idea a day.

Waiting costs twice.

Buy term cover later, and age can make it costlier.
Wait too long, and one diagnosis can change insurability too: exclusion, loading, or even a decline.

Money is one cost. Insurability is the other.
Save this.

Family floater is cheaper. That is true.

But the trade-off is one shared sum insured. One big claim by one family member can leave less cover for everyone else in that policy year.

Individual cover costs more, but each person gets their own bucket. Save this.

Planning a pregnancy, then buying maternity cover, is usually too late.

Most policies start maternity benefits only after 2-4 years. Normal delivery and C-section can have separate sub-limits, and newborn cover details matter too. Check the policy wording.

24-hour stay is not the real test.

Dialysis, chemotherapy, cataract, some endoscopies can be covered as day-care treatments even without overnight admission.

Check your policy lists day-care treatment. Save this. #HealthInsurance

Planned surgery is not the same as an emergency claim.

For planned admission, pre-authorisation is usually requested several days earlier.
For emergency admission, intimation is usually needed within hours.

This one difference prevents many cashless delays. Save this.

Reimbursement claim? Keep this ready:
discharge summary, final bill, payment receipts, prescriptions, investigation reports, doctor's advice, ID proof, bank details.
Originals are usually needed. Keep copies too.
Save this.

Claim delayed, so you keep calling only the TPA?

The TPA handles claim administration and the network hospital list. But the risk and final decision sit with the insurer.

So if things stall, escalation does not stop at the TPA. Ask me anything about health cover.

Child plan first, retired parent first, earning member later: backwards.

Insurance should usually start where the household income starts. If that income stops, the family budget takes the hit first.

Build outward after that.
Follow for one clear insurance idea a day.

Insurance and investment are two different jobs.

Insurance takes the hit from a risk you cannot afford.
Investing grows money over time.

Mix them, and both jobs often get weaker. Protection secures the plan; investing builds it. Save this.

Cheapest premium can become the costliest claim.

Low price often hides co-pay, room-rent caps, sub-limits, or long exclusion lists. Compare cover and conditions first. If the cover is truly similar, then compare price.

Save this.

Claim-free year? Your health cover may have quietly grown.

Many plans add a no-claim bonus to your sum insured, up to a cap. After a claim, some plans reduce that bonus again.

Good benefit. Easy detail to miss. Check the policy wording. Save this.

Unhappy with your health insurer? Don’t just stop paying.

Apply for portability in the renewal window, commonly 30-60 days before renewal. If accepted, you can carry waiting-period credit. Let the policy lapse, and you may restart from zero.

Save this.

One hospitalisation can empty a family floater.

Restoration benefit refills the sum insured after that. Often once, usually for a different member or a different illness. Some plans allow unlimited refills.

Check the policy wording. Save this.

Flight delayed? The payout is usually not open-ended.

Most travel policies start only after a stated delay threshold, then pay a fixed amount per day up to a cap. Airline compensation is counted separately too.

Read that threshold before buying. Save this.

Going to the mountains or underwater? Standard travel insurance may cover the trip, but not trekking at altitude, skiing, rafting, or scuba unless you bought the right add-on.

This detail decides whether rescue is covered. Save this. #TravelInsurance

Sending your child abroad to study? A tourist policy is the wrong tool.

Student travel plans are built for university medical requirements, longer stays, and extras like study interruption or sponsor protection.

Save this. #TravelInsurance

“Best” child plan? Not always.

A child plan mixes a small insurance cover with an investment.
Before buying, compare it side by side with a term plan plus a separate investment.

The better fit depends on the comparison. Save this.

Claims are rejected at random is a myth.

The outcome usually turns on 3 things: what you disclosed, what waiting periods apply, and what the policy excludes.

Insurers have to state a reason. Check the policy wording. Save this.

Buying insurance online is always cheaper.
Usually not for the same product.
What changes is the cover, the fine print, and whether you have someone to call at claim time. Compare guidance and service too, not just price. Save this.

Rider offered at the last screen? Pause.

Accidental death, critical illness, waiver of premium: each does one narrow job, and each adds to the premium.

Buy a rider for a risk you actually carry, not just because it is there.
Save this.

Your health policy will handle critical illness anyway. Myth.

Critical illness cover pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a listed condition. Hospitalisation cover pays treatment bills.

Different jobs. Check your policy wording. Save this.

Can’t pay the premium because income stopped?

A waiver-of-premium rider can keep the term policy running if you become disabled or critically ill. But it works only as the policy defines disability and illness. Check the policy wording.

Save this.

Big health cover does not always need one big premium.

A modest base policy handles the first layer.
A super top-up kicks in after the deductible and counts total claims in the year, not each claim separately.

Save this.

60 months of continuous cover can matter.

Under IRDAI norms, after a long continuous period, a claim generally cannot be contested except for proven fraud or misrepresentation.

One more reason: don’t let your policy lapse. Save this.

Hospital bill looked fine till the “small items” showed up?

Gloves, syringes, cotton, implants: these consumables can quietly add up, and many older plans did not pay them.

Before comparing premiums, ask one thing: are consumables covered? Check the policy wording.
Save this.

Claims get rejected at the hospital. Usually, the mistake happened while buying.

Missed a pre-existing condition, claimed before waiting period, chose a treatment the policy excludes, or sent mismatched papers.

Most of this is avoidable. Save this.

Hospital bill was Rs X, claim paid less, and it feels random.

Usually it is not. Part may be non-payable, cut for a higher room category, or capped by a sub-limit.

Ask for the claim settlement sheet. Read it line by line. Save this.

Claim gone wrong? Don’t stop at an angry phone call.

Use the free escalation ladder:
insurer’s grievance redressal officer
then IRDAI’s grievance portal
then the Insurance Ombudsman for eligible complaints.

Ask me anything about health cover.

Bought a policy after the diagnosis? Awkward truth: it usually won’t help for that same illness.

Why: waiting periods, medical underwriting, and exclusions apply from day one. Insurance works best before the emergency, not inside it.

Save this.

Five policies from five places sounds flexible. Until renewal month or claim time.

One advisor keeps the family’s cover in view, reminders in one place, and gives you one person to call when papers start flying.

Follow for one clear insurance idea a day.

One evening over chai can fix a lot.

Check 4 things together: sum insured, renewal dates, nominees, and whether a new loan or a new child changed the cover you need.

Small ritual, fewer surprises later.

Follow for one clear insurance idea a day.

Treatment at home can be covered.

If the patient cannot be moved, or no hospital bed is available, some health plans may allow domiciliary hospitalisation.

Useful benefit. Often capped. Check the policy wording. Save this.

Emergency means you call the ambulance, not compare plans.

Good news: road ambulance charges are part of many health covers, usually within a limit. Air ambulance is often capped much lower or excluded.

Check yours before the rush. Save this.
